That is why row-level security in the database is the stronger control - it applies to every connection regardless of how the query was written - with the query filter as a convenience layer on top.

followups.q: How do you handle the noisy neighbour problem in a pooled model?
followups.a: Cap what any one tenant can consume: per-tenant rate limits at the API, a concurrency cap so one tenant cannot occupy all workers, and query timeouts so a single expensive report cannot dominate. Monitor per-tenant usage so you can see it happening rather than discovering it as a general slowdown. When a tenant consistently exceeds what pooling can absorb, that is the signal to move them to dedicated resources - which is why the hybrid model tends to emerge naturally rather than being designed up front.

question: Design a social feed. Fan-out on write or fan-out on read?
answer:
The two approaches put the cost in opposite places, and the right answer is usually both.

**Fan-out on write (push).** When someone posts, write a copy into every follower s feed. Reads are then a single lookup on a precomputed list - fast and cheap, which matters because reads vastly outnumber writes. The cost is write amplification: a user with a million followers generates a million writes for one post, which is slow and expensive, and most of those feeds are never read.

**Fan-out on read (pull).** Store posts once; build the feed at read time by querying the people you follow and merging. Writes are trivial. Reads are expensive and get worse the more people you follow, and reads are the common operation - so this scales badly for the main use case.

**The hybrid is what production systems actually do:** fan out on write for ordinary accounts, and handle high-follower accounts on read. A user s feed is then the merge of their precomputed list plus a live query for the handful of celebrities they follow. That keeps write amplification bounded and reads cheap.

**The other decisions that matter as much:**
- **Inactive users.** Do not fan out to accounts that have not opened the app in months - a large share of writes otherwise go to feeds nobody reads. Backfill on their return.
- **Cursor pagination**, because a feed is the canonical case where offset paging duplicates and skips items as new posts arrive.
- **Ranking versus chronology.** A ranked feed cannot be a simple precomputed list; you fan out candidates and rank at read time, which shifts work back to reads deliberately.
- **Deletes and privacy changes** must propagate to every copied entry, which is the ongoing cost of denormalising.

followups.q: What storage would you use for the precomputed feeds?
followups.a: Something optimised for append and range reads by key - a Redis sorted set per user keyed by timestamp is the common choice for the hot window, backed by a wide-column store such as Cassandra for the longer tail. The important property is that you only keep a bounded window per user, typically a few hundred entries, because nobody scrolls further and unbounded feeds multiply storage by the follower graph. Anything older is served by falling back to a query.

followups.q: How do you handle the moment a user follows someone new?
followups.a: Backfill their feed with that person s recent posts, or accept that the new follow only affects future posts. Backfilling is better for the experience - the feed immediately reflects the change - and it is a bounded operation since you only need the recent window. The case to watch is a bulk import or someone following thousands of accounts at once, which turns a user action into a large amount of work, so it belongs on a queue with rate limiting rather than inline in the request.

question: Design a system that lets users upload and stream video.
answer:
Video is the case where the naive design - accept the file, store it, serve it - fails at every stage, so the shape is a pipeline.

**Upload.** Direct to object storage with a pre-signed URL, never through the application. Large files need **resumable, chunked upload** because mobile connections drop - the client uploads parts and can resume from the last acknowledged part rather than restarting a 2GB transfer.

**Ingest and validate.** The upload completing raises an event. A worker validates the container and codec, checks duration and dimensions, and scans it. The upload target is a quarantine bucket nothing else reads from.

**Transcode.** This is the core of it. One source file becomes a ladder of renditions - several resolutions and bitrates - packaged for adaptive streaming with HLS or DASH. That is what lets a player switch quality as bandwidth changes, and it is why you cannot just serve the original MP4. Transcoding is CPU-intensive and bursty, so it belongs on a queue with workers that scale, and segments of a long video can be transcoded in parallel.

**Storage and delivery.** Renditions and segments go to object storage behind a CDN - essential, because video is large and bandwidth from origin is expensive and slow. Thumbnails and a preview sprite are generated in the same pipeline.

**Playback.** The player requests a manifest listing the renditions and picks one based on measured bandwidth, adjusting as it goes. Signed, expiring URLs if the content is protected, and DRM if licensing requires it.

**The state to track throughout:** the video has a status - uploaded, validating, transcoding, ready, failed - surfaced to the user, because transcoding takes minutes and silence looks broken.

followups.q: Why can you not just serve the original file with HTTP range requests?
followups.a: You can, and it works for small clips - the browser fetches byte ranges and seeks. It fails for real video because there is one quality: a user on a poor connection either buffers constantly or cannot play at all, and a mobile user downloads a 4K file to a small screen. Adaptive streaming exists to solve exactly that by letting the player switch renditions mid-playback. Serving the original also means no control over codec compatibility across devices, which is why transcoding is unavoidable rather than an optimisation.

followups.q: How do you handle a transcode that fails halfway through a long video?
followups.a: Segment the work so it is resumable - split the source into chunks, transcode each independently, and record which are complete, so a failure retries one chunk rather than the whole file. That also gives you parallelism, which is what makes a long video finish in reasonable time. The job needs an overall timeout and a dead-letter path so a genuinely broken source file is surfaced to the user as a failure rather than retrying forever, and the partial output must be cleaned up so storage does not fill with abandoned renditions.

question: Design a system that runs millions of user-scheduled reminders at the right time.
answer:
The naive design - a table of reminders and a job polling "where due <= now" every minute - works to a point and then falls over, because the query scans an ever-growing table and the due-now set arrives in bursts at round times like 9:00.

**The shape I would build:**

1. **Partition by time.** Store reminders bucketed into time windows - a table partitioned by due date, or keys shaped so a due-minute is a direct lookup. The scheduler then reads one bucket rather than querying the whole table, so cost is proportional to what is due rather than to what exists.
2. **A two-tier approach.** A durable store holds everything; a short-horizon queue holds only the next few minutes of work. A loader moves items from the store into the queue as their window approaches, which keeps the hot path small.
3. **Use the infrastructure where it fits.** Service Bus scheduled messages and delayed queues hand the timing problem to the broker, which is attractive for horizons of hours or days. The limit is cancellation and update - a user changing a reminder means finding and cancelling a scheduled message, which is awkward at volume, so the durable store remains the source of truth.
4. **Spread the bursts.** Everything due at 09:00 arrives at once, so the workers must scale and the downstream - push notification services, email providers - must be rate limited. Jittering delivery by a few seconds where the product tolerates it flattens the spike enormously.
5. **Claim work atomically** so several workers take disjoint batches - `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or an equivalent claim with a lease - and make delivery idempotent, because a worker crashing after sending and before marking will redeliver.

**And handle the clock properly:** store the user s timezone and the intended local time, not just a UTC instant, or a daily 9am reminder drifts by an hour at DST.

followups.q: Why store local time plus timezone rather than a computed UTC instant?
followups.a: Because a recurring reminder at 9am local must remain 9am after a DST transition, and a UTC instant computed today will be an hour out after the clocks change. Storing the intended local time with the IANA zone identifier lets you resolve the correct instant at scheduling time for each occurrence. It also survives a government changing the rules, which happens more often than people expect - a stored offset is a snapshot of a rule, while a zone identifier is a reference to the current rules.

followups.q: How do you handle a user editing or cancelling a reminder that is already in the short-horizon queue?
followups.a: Treat the durable store as authoritative and the queue as a hint: when the worker picks up an item, it re-reads the reminder and checks it is still due and still active before sending. That way a cancellation only has to update the store, and the stale queue entry is discarded harmlessly on pickup. Trying to remove the message from the queue instead couples you to the broker s capabilities and races with the worker already having taken it.
